In the Heart of the Sea Community Reading: Q&A with Nat Philbrick, Niles Parker, & Michael Harrison

The Community Reading of Nathaniel Philbrick’s award-winning bestseller “In the Heart of the Sea” featured a lively Q&A panel with Nat Philbrick, NHA Executive Director Niles Parker, and NHA Chief Curator Michael Harrison at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. They discussed the book, the movie based on the book, the exhibitions at the museum inspired by the tragedy of the whaleship Essex and Philbrick’s book, and how each came to be. A New York Times bestseller, “In the Heart of the Sea,” follows the crew members of Nantucket’s whaleship Essex after it was brutally taken down by a sperm whale in the Pacific Ocean. Crew members drifted at sea for more than 90 days in tiny lifeboats, with only eight surviving at the end of their 4,500-mile journey. The book was published in 2000 and won the National Book Award for nonfiction. It was the basis of the 2015 movie of the same title directed by Ron Howard. The book also inspired a 2001 Dateline special on NBC as well as the 2010 PBS American Experience film “Into the Deep” by Ric Burns. In 2019, the National Endowment for the Arts added the book to their ever-growing library of 32 titles in the NEA Big Read program under which libraries and non-profits can apply for grants in order to develop in-depth, community-wide programming around a common book. Nathaniel Philbrick was born in Boston, Massachusetts, and grew up in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where he attended Linden Elementary School and Taylor Allderdice High School. He earned a BA in English from Brown University and an MA in America Literature from Duke University, where he was a James B. Duke Fellow. He was Brown University’s first Intercollegiate All-American sailor in 1978, the same year he won the Sunfish North Americans in Barrington, RI. After working as an editor at Sailing World magazine, he wrote and edited several books about sailing, including “The Passionate Sailor,” “Second Wind,” and “Yaahting: A Parody.” Niles Parker is the Gosnell Executive Director at the Nantucket Historical Association since 2022. He previously held the position as the Robyn and John Davis Chief Curator at the NHA from 1999 to 2006, as well as acting Executive Director from 2005 to 2006. He played a significant role in the Whaling Museum’s major expansion and renovation project in 2005. Prior to his current position, he was Executive Director at the Maine Discovery Museum, where he led the organization through two strategic planning processes, resulting in a dynamic shift toward expanded programming and increased revenues. He also was one of the founders of the Maine Science Festival and developed strong partnerships with surrounding universities and non-profits. Parker held the position of Executive Director of the Penobscot Marine Museum from 2006 to 2010, where he managed a regional museum and fourteen properties, five of which are on the National Register of Historic Places. Michael R. Harrison is Chief Curator & Obed Macy Research Chair at the Nantucket Historical Association. He has held curatorial positions at the National Building Museum, the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, and the Glasgow Museum of Transport. He is the author of numerous books and articles, as well as nearly seventy historical reports on maritime, architectural, and engineering topics for U.S. National Park Service’s Heritage Documentation Programs. He is a graduate of the University of Pennsylvania and holds a master’s degree in museum studies from the George Washington University.

Life Aboard a Whaleship at the Nantucket Whaling Museum

What was it like to live aboard a whaleship and hunt for whales in the 19th century? It’s a story that has been told at the Nantucket Whaling Museum since the 1930s, when retired whaling captain George Grant became the first “custodian” of the Whaling Museum and shared his first-hand whaling experiences with museum visitors. That began a long-standing tradition of telling this same story, passed down to each new generation of museum guides. In 2024, Life Aboard a Whaleship, has been updated to explain why and how Nantucketers turned to whaling and to tell the story of a whaling voyage aboard the whaleship Edward Cary, 1854-58. This special program was part of Multilingual Day at the Nantucket Whaling Museum and was presented in English and American Sign Language (ASL) Presenter: Robert Kucharavy, Museum Guide, Nantucket Historical Association ASL Interpreter: Diana Graves, Educator, Nantucket Public Schools

Tony Sarg Community Day on Nantucket

The Nantucket Historical Association hosted Sarg Community Day on Monday, August 5, 2024 at Children’s Beach on Nantucket. Bringing a recreation of Tony Sarg’s 75-foot sea monster balloon to the island for all to see, enjoy, and take photos with. Sarg Community Day offered family-friendly activities, including a Nanpuppets performance, a kazoo parade with Nantucket Community Music Center and crafts exploring the art of puppetry. Tony Sarg (1880-1942) is known as the father of modern puppetry in North America and the originator of the iconic Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade balloons. Sarg was an accomplished illustrator, animator, designer, and nimble entrepreneur who summered on, and took inspiration from, Nantucket for nearly twenty years. In the summer of 1937, Sarg orchestrated a media hoax on Nantucket with his sea monster balloon. He planned various spottings around the island, including footprints on the beach and sightings of a creature in the water. A few days later, Sarg displayed his massive sea monster balloon, which he named “Morton,” on Francis Street Beach for locals and tourists to be wowed by, and it soon became known as the “event of the summer.” To recreate this moment in history, the NHA worked with Bill Smith of Smith Special Productions and Balloonworks to create a modern day, “Morton.” This special event is part of the Nantucket Historical Association’s Summer of Sarg and complements the Tony Sarg: Genius at Play exhibition at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. Learn more about the exhibition open through 2024 at https://nha.org/whats-on/exhibitions/featured-exhibitions/tony-sarg-genius-at-play/. Learn more about Tony Sarg on the NHA’s YouTube channel - https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLjgJVmnztYsRB_un_aemFMpW664-6HE_Z&si=h2qdbLclmrGRz5Nw

USS Nantucket Official Crest Unveiling at the Nantucket Whaling Museum

The Nantucket Historical Association hosts the formal unveiling ceremony of the USS Nantucket’s official crest, September 20 at 4pm at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. The United States Navy (USN) christened one of its newest Freedom-variant littoral combat ships (LCS), the USS Nantucket (LCS 27), earlier this summer on August 7, in Marinette, Wisconsin. “The USS Nantucket is the third U.S. Navy ship commissioned to honor the maritime history and spirit of Nantucket,” said Acting Secretary of the Navy Thomas Harker. “I have no doubt the Sailors of USS Nantucket (LCS 27) will carry on the proud legacy from generations past in preserving sea lanes, countering instability, and maintaining our maritime superiority.” The USS Nantucket Commissioning Committee and the Prospective Commanding Officer will present the ship’s official crest and discuss how they symbolized Nantucket history within it. Attendees will learn about planning efforts for the Commissioning Ceremony and meet the Prospective Commanding Officer. The Chairman of the Commissioning Committee, Robert Gerosa, Commander, USN (Ret), a former Commanding Officer of USS Constitution, will be the MC host. The USS Constitution Color Guard, the Commodore for Littoral Combat Ships Squadron Two, CAPT David Miller, USN, and the Prospective Commanding Officer of USS Nantucket, Commander Kari Yakubisin, USN will be present. Also attending will be summer resident and ship sponsor and christener Polly Spencer, wife of Richard V. Spencer, the 76th Secretary of the U.S. Navy from 2017 to 2019.

200th Anniversary of the Sinking of the Whaleship Essex with Nathaniel Philbrick

On November 20, 1820, the ill-fated whaleship Essex was struck by a whale, stranding its crew in three tiny whaleboats in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, 1,300 miles from the nearest land. In commemoration of the 200th anniversary of this tragedy, the Nantucket Historical Association hosted this virtual event with award-winning best-selling author Nathaniel Philbrick in conversation with Michael Harrison, NHA Obed Macy Research Chair. The discussion reflects on the legacy of the Essex tragedy and the fate of its survivors. It is most appropriate that Nat Philbrick help bring this gripping story to life in this apt setting under the whale skeleton in Gosnell Hall at the Nantucket Whaling Museum in full view of the appropriately-small whaleboat. Philbrick’s New York Times bestseller, “In the Heart of the Sea,” published in 2000 and which won the National Book Award for nonfiction, has been recognized as a monumental work of history forever placing the Essex tragedy in the American historical canon.

Juneteenth Commemoration, 2020, at the Nantucket Historical Association

Please join Nantucket Historical Association staff and community members for a commemoration of Juneteenth, a holiday celebrating the emancipation of those who had been enslaved in the United States. It is commemorated on the anniversary date of the June 19, 1865 announcement by Union Army general Gordon Granger, proclaiming freedom from slavery in Texas. Our program remembers the day through selected readings including: The Significance of Juneteenth Disturber of Tradition, A Portrait of Anna Gardner (selected passage read by author, Barbara White) The Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (selected passages) Emancipation Proclamation (extract) For information on the Black history resources currently digitized in the NHA collections, please visit the Black History Portal at https://nha.org/research/nantucket-history/history-topic/black-history/

Extraordinary Nantucket Women, at the Nantucket Whaling Museum

This 2018 performance at the Nantucket Whaling Museum highlights the lives of fifteen extraordinary women from the 17th through the 20th century on Nantucket. From its earliest days, dating back to the mid-1600s, Nantucketers have made their own way in the world. This is particularly true of the women who made their homes here. From the outset, men and women worked equally hard to make the fledgling settlement survive. When whaling became the dominant industry, whaling husbands would leave the island for years at a time, often, 3-5 years. At any given time, the women probably outnumbered the men four to one. Women had to fill the breach and did so in remarkable ways, raising their large families, managing households and running businesses in town, and found the time to become involved in the social movements of the day. William Oliver Stevens, an American author and professor, wrote, “Indeed, it is probable that no other community in America of the size of Nantucket has ever given the country so many extraordinary women.” The notable women include: Mary Coffin Starbuck (1645-1717) Abiah Folger Franklin (1667-1752) Kezia Folger Coffin (1772-1798) Lucretia Coffin Mott (1793-1880) Eliza Ann Chase McCleave (1811-1895) Susan Veeder (1816-1897) Maria Mitchell (1818-1889) Rebecca Ann Johnson (1829-??) Mary Ellen Pleasant (ca. 1812-1904) Eliza Starbuck Barney (1802-1889) Anna Gardner (1816-1901) Lydia Folger Fowler, M.D. (1822-1879) Margaret Getchell (1841-1880) Hanna Monaghan (1889-1972) Mildred Jewitt “Madaket Millie” (1907-1990) Also featuring the “Nantucket Girl’s Song” based on a witty poem found in the journal kept by Eliza Brock, wife of Peter C. Brock, master of the Nantucket ship Lexington on a whaling voyage from May 1853 to June 1856. It sums up how many women felt about their husbands being off on whaling voyages for years at a time. Songwriter Susan J. Berman set this poem to music and added a verse of her own.

The Hunt for Whales, presented at the Nantucket Whaling Museum

The story of what it was like to hunt for whales in the 18th-19th centuries has been told since the 1930s when retired whaling captain George Grant became the first curator of the Nantucket Whaling Museum and shared his first-hand whaling experiences with museum visitors. That began a long-standing tradition of telling this story passed down to each new generation of museum interpreters. This version of “The Hunt for Whales” was created as a multi-media object-theater presentation to celebrate the opening of the new Nantucket Whaling Museum in 2005 and has been presented daily in Gosnell Hall under the whale skeleton. The lecture has evolved over time with corrected and additional information. Today in 2025, it is known as “Life Aboard a Whaleship.” This version can be viewed at https://youtu.be/0n2cRgXW-QQ. NOTE: The following corrections to this video were provided by Robert Rocha from the New Bedford Whaling Museum in 2023. The science of sperm whale ecology should be adjusted as follows: - Right whales don’t just feed at the surface. - Sperm whales cannot hold their breath for two hours. - Their eyesight is not poor. It certainly is not their primary means of picturing what’s around them. But it is well-adapted for seeing in water and they are able to pick up on visual cues, including bioluminescence. - The presenter stated that sperm whales grab giant squid and shoot to the surface so that the squid will explode in the whale’s mouth. Sperm whales, and deep diving toothed whales in general, do not ascend in this fashion. Research has demonstrated that they ascend more deliberately, taking time to rest or swim horizontally and equilibrate the gases in their blood. Giant squid don’t have a gas-filled cavity, so there’s no structure that will expand and explode. If this were the case, the colossal squid, a deep-sea species, caught by New Zealand fishermen in 2007 would have exploded, or we’d never see giant squid washed up on beaches, intact. - Sperm whales have never been recorded at two miles of depth. - There’s no proof that giant squid are their favorite food. They’ll eat whatever squid is available. - Sperm whales weren’t hunted north of the Aleutian Islands. - Being stabbed with a harpoon likely does hurt the whale. - They do not have many feet of blubber. In the biggest of sperm whales, the blubber might be nearly 12“ thick. But it’s normally thinner than that. - When talking about ‘Chimney’s Afire’, which the presenter called “There’s Fire in the Chimney,” she said that the whale is no longer spouting water or air…whales don’t spout water. Also - There’s 1800 feet of line in a tub, not 1500. - The cooper and the carpenter are not the same person ________________________________________________ Presenter: Kirsten Gamble Paintings, photographs and manuscripts: Nantucket Historical Association Collections Additional paintings by Rodney Charman, courtesy of the Albert F. Egan, Jr. & Dorothy H. Nantucket-Cape Verde Connection: Heritage

Heritage: “Our grandchildren need to know that we’re proud to be Cape Verdean.” People of the Cape Verde archipelago and their descendants have been part of the story of Nantucket since the early nineteenth century. While diminished in numbers from early days, the Nantucket Cape Verdean community today is made up of significant contributors to education, health care, service to the community, government, business, trades, music, and cuisine, assuring that anyone in their expanded spheres are well fed. They are a microcosm of the best of Nantucket’s community spirit, subtly proud of their Cape Verde heritage. This short film is based on recently conducted oral histories with members of Nantucket’s Cape Verdean community. Special thanks to those who shared their stories: Kenneth DeLuze, Dominic Duarte, Kezia Duarte, Mary Fernandes, Anthony “Rocky” Fox, Viola Cabral Howard, Leslie Gomes Preston, Edmund “Rookie” Ramos, Pauline Cabral Singleton, Theran Singleton, and Claudia Stanley. Interviews conducted by Frances Karttunen for the Nantucket Historical Association. Learn more about the Nantucket-Cape Verde connection at https://nha.org/research/nantucket-history/history-topic/cape-verdean-heritage-on-nantucket/. Music: “Morna di Freddie” performed by Verdatones

Mrs. Perry: The Life of Edith Correia Perry, Cape Verdean Matriarch

A pillar in the Nantucket Cape Verdean community, Edith Correia Perry (1908-1992) came to Nantucket as an infant. Edith worked in the Roberts House and St. Mary’s Church, and her special devotion to service and care eventually drew her to Our Island Home where she worked for many years. She and her husband were also know for establishing a 33-acre farm outside of town and for building a popular night club called 30 Acres on the property. It was a happening place for decades. At the time of her death, Edith was survived by twelve children, forty-seven grandchildren and three great-grandchildren. She is remembered for her cheerful and warm demeanor, a remarkable mother figure and caregiver to everyone who knew her. This short film by Nantucket High School student Anna Popnikolova was produced as part of the 2022 TeenView Labs, an educational filmmaking program established by the Nantucket Film Festival in partnership with Nantucket Community Television (NCTV).

Nantucket’s Portuguese Heritage with Frances Karttunen

Whaling brought men from the Cape Verde Islands and the Azores to Nantucket. Later, opportunities for a better life brought whole families to Nantucket, where their contributions have added greatly to our culture and economy. Frances Karttunen talks about how a new generation of their sons and daughters have benefited Nantucket as part of the Food for Thought Lecture Series at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. Twelfth-generation Nantucketer Frances Karttunen was educated in the local public schools. She received a bachelor’s degree with honors from Radcliffe College and a Ph.D. in linguistics from Indiana University. She held the position of Senior University Research Scientist at the Linguistics Research Center at the University of Texas, at Austin, and also served as Program Director for Linguistics at the National Science Foundation. She has been awarded three Fulbright fellowships, all in Finland. One of Dr. Karttunen’s grandparents was a native Nantucketer and the other an immigrant from Finland. The difficulties and adjustments they and their family members encountered were among the inspirations for her earlier book Between Worlds and her later book, The Other Islanders: People Who Pulled Nantucket’s Oars. She is also the author of numerous other books and articles about Nantucket.

Artists Who Championed the American Revolution with Zara Anishanslin

Zara Anishanslin, The Painter’s Fire: A Forgotten History of the Artists Who Championed the American Revolution The war that we now call the American Revolution was not only fought in the colonies by soldiers with muskets and bayonets. On both sides of the Atlantic, artists also played an integral role in forging revolutionary ideals. Art historian and author Zara Anishanslin discusses the inspiring stories and intertwined lives of three of these largely forgotten Patriot artists: Robert Edge Pine, Prince Demah, and Patience Wright. They defied the British monarchy, armed with paint, canvas, wax, and espionage while risking their lives and reputations to support the cause of liberty. These stories and more are featured in her new book “The Painter’s Fire: A Forgotten History of the Artists Who Championed the American Revolution.” Zara Anishanslin is Professor of History and Art History at the University of Delaware, where she also is Director of its Museum Studies and Public Engagement Program. She previously taught at CUNY and at Columbia and was a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of History at Johns Hopkins. Her award-winning first book, Portrait of a Woman in Silk: Hidden Histories of the British Atlantic World, was published by Yale University Press in 2016. Her new book, The Painter’s Fire: A Forgotten History of the Artists Who Championed the American Revolution (Harvard University Press, July 2025) has been featured in Smithsonian Magazine, USA Today, and the Wall Street Journal and made the 2026 Cundhill Prize in History Longlist. While researching The Painter’s Fire, she was a Mount Vernon Georgian Papers Fellow at the Royal Archives at Windsor Castle, a Davis Center Fellow in Princeton’s History Department, a Fellow at the American Antiquarian Society and the Massachusetts Historical Society, a Mellon/ACLS Scholars & Society Fellow with the Museum of the American Revolution, and a Fellow at the David Center for the American Revolution at the American Philosophical Society. An avid public historian, her work has appeared in Time Magazine, Mount Vernon Magazine, Colonial Williamsburg’s Trend and Tradition Magazine, and the Washington Post. She often works with museums on exhibitions, including the reinstallation of the Early American Wing at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. She is creator/co-host of the podcast “Thing 4 Things: The History Podcast Where Things Matter and Stuff Happens” (season 1, “The Stuff of Revolution” streaming now wherever you listen to podcasts). But according to her children, the only cool thing on her CV is that she served as Material Culture Consult for Lin-Manuel Miranda’s show, “Hamilton: The Exhibition.”

Freedom & Equality in the Revolutionary Atlantic World with Ronald Angelo Johnson

From his new book “Entangled Alliances: Racialized Freedom and Atlantic Diplomacy during the American Revolution” (Cornell University Press), historian Ronald Angelo Johnson discusses the myriad of ways US patriots and Black Atlantic inhabitants across North American and the Caribbean island of Saint-Domingue (later Haiti) sought and fought for freedom and equality during the American Revolution. Presented for the Nantucket Historical Association at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. Ronald Angelo Johnson is the Ralph and Bessie Mae Lynn Professor of History at Baylor University. He is the author of “Diplomacy in Black and White: John Adams”, “Toussaint Louverture”, and “Their Atlantic Alliances” and the co-editor of the book “In Search of Liberty: African American Internationalism in the Nineteenth-Century Atlantic World”.

Nantucket During the American Revolution with Julie O’Leary

This lecture presented by geneologist and author Julie Folger O-Leary explores how the first years of the American Revolution reshaped life on Nantucket, from the pressures of being neutral in a time of war to the struggles of food shortages, the hard winter, and attacks on the island. She also brings individual stories to life, featuring Daniel Prior, sailor on the Bon Homme Richard; Frederick Folger, Town Clerk of Nantucket during the Revolution and ancestor of the speaker; and Aaron Snow, a private who settled on the island after serving in the war. Growing up in Kansas, Julie Folger O’Leary found it hard to believe that she had Nantucket roots. Through research, Julie was able to prove that she is a descendant of several original settlers of Nantucket, including Coffin, Coleman, Gardner, Marshall, Shattuck, Swain, as well as Folger. Through research for the book, The American Revolution on Cape Cod and the Islands, Julie was able to piece together a picture of what her Nantucket ancestors experienced during those difficult years of being a neutral island during the Revolution, including the life of her 5th Great Grandfather, Frederick Folger, Esq., who served as the Town Clerk during the American Revolution and who signed the Treaty of Neutrality. Julie has traced her family genealogy and joined the Colonial Dames through Tristram Coffin and the Daughters of the American Revolution, through Jonathan Moore, a Private in George Washington’s Lifeguard. She is past Registrar of the Lexington MA chapter of DAR and a member of the Civil War Daughters through Jacob Moore of Ohio; she has also joined the First Families groups for Oklahoma and Nebraska. She is serving on the Lex250 Commission, which has the charge of planning events for the celebration of the Battle of Lexington for 2025 and 2026. While serving as Registrar for the Lexington Chapter of DAR, she found it rewarding to help others connect to their heritage and learn about their family stories. Julie also is on the board for the Nims family Association of Deerfield, MA and is a member of the Cape Cod Genealogy Society. She is the author of six different chapters in the Revolution book.

Nantucket and the American Revolution - Part 1

Muster your friends and family, gather and listen close as the Nantucket Gam celebrates America’s 250th anniversary with a tale of Nantucket during the American Revolution! Join us for a tale of economic collapse, Quakerism, smuggling, divided loyalties and uneasy neutrality on our lonely island 30 miles out to sea. How does an island dependent on a single industry navigate the conflict between the colonies and London? Who would you be - Patriot, Privateer, Loyalist or Smuggler? Learn all about it in part one of our two-part series on Nantucket and the American Revolution.

The American Revolution with Nathaniel Philbrick

Author and historian Nathaniel Philbrick shares his insights and discoveries from 13 years of research and writing on George Washington and the American Revolution. Nathaniel Philbrick is the author of eight New York Times bestselling works of American history, including In the Heart of the Sea, winner of the 2000 National Book Award and the basis of the 2015 movie of the same title directed by Ron Howard; Mayflower, a finalist for the 2007 Pulitzer Prize in History; a trilogy about the American Revolution that includes Valiant Ambition, winner of the George Washington Book Prize; and his latest, Travels with George. Philbrick’s writing has appeared in Vanity Fair, the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Los Angeles Times, and the Boston Globe. He has appeared on the Today Show, The Morning Show, Dateline, PBS’s American Experience, C-SPAN, and NPR. He and his wife Melissa have lived on Nantucket Island since 1986. This lecture was presented for the Nantucket Historical Association at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Nantucket Quakers, Wales and the Revolutionary Wars with Dr. Richard C. Allen

Join Dr. Richard Allen, NHA Geoffrey and Elizabeth Thayer Verney Fellow, for a look inside his research project. Presented at the Nantucket Whaling Museum for the Nantucket Historical Association. In a recent article, it was argued that the American Revolutionary Wars not only saw a shift in mid-Atlantic politics but also occasioned a transformation in the economic networks that had existed from the opening up of the American colonies in the seventeenth century. Specific attention was drawn to the Nantucket Quaker whalers whose determination to carry on their trade while attempting to maintain neutrality led to the sequestration of their goods and ships, occupation of their homes, and ultimately a repositioning of their industry. This paper rehearses some of those arguments and develops the deep levels of negotiation between the American, British, and French governments, and the Nantucketers, especially the Rotch family who relocated to Dunkerque and others who settled in Milford Haven, West Wales. Dr. Richard C. Allen is an Early Modern social historian. Between 2007 and 2008 he was the Fulbright-Robertson Visiting Professor of British History at Westminster College, Missouri, and he is currently the Partnership Development Manager at Woodbrooke {Quaker} College, Birmingham, UK, and postgraduate research supervisor for the college in association with the School of Theology and Religion, University of Birmingham. He was a Reader (Associate Professor) and Head of History at the University of Wales, Newport for many years. He is now a visiting research fellow at Newcastle University, UK, and an Honorary Senior Lecturer at The Australian National University, Humanities Research Centre, Canberra, Australia.

Mining Climate Clues from Ships’ Logs

Dr. Timothy Walker, Professor of History at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, and oceanographer Dr. Caroline Ummenhofer from Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, highlight how weather records contained in ship logbooks from American whaling voyages can be used to assess shifting wind and weather patterns. A treasure trove of unexploited ship logbooks spanning the period 1790 to 1910 exists in several New England archives, such as the Nantucket Historical Association, New Bedford Whaling Museum, Providence Public Library, and Falmouth Historical Society. The logbooks, often covering multi-year voyages to some of the most remote waters around the globe, contain systematic daily weather observations, such as wind strength/direction, rainfall, and cloudiness. The results demonstrate that the historical records provide an important long-term context for changing wind and weather patterns over the world’s oceans, lacking observational records during the 18th-19th centuries. The presentation focuses on challenges and opportunities for climate research through data rescue and digitization of these under-utilized historical ship logbooks. Presented at the Nantucket Whaling Museum for the Nantucket Historical Association. Caroline Ummenhofer received a Joint Honours B.Sc. in Marine Biology and Physical Oceanography from Bangor University, UK, and a PhD in Applied Mathematics from the University of New South Wales, Australia, specializing in climate modeling. She joined Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution as faculty in 2012. Her research focuses on the ocean’s role in extreme events, such as droughts and floods, and their impact on human and natural systems. She has participated in art-science collaborations at museum exhibits about marine heatwaves and the oceanic water cycle, and provided educational resources on extreme weather for K-12 schools serving students around the world. Dr. Timothy Walker (Hiram College, 1986; MA/Ph.D. Boston University 2001), Professor of History at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, is a scholar of maritime history, colonial overseas expansion, and trans-oceanic slave trading. Walker is a guest investigator of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, drawing historic climate data from archived whaling logbooks, Portuguese colonial, and other maritime documentation. He is a contributing faculty member of the Munson Institute of Maritime Studies, affiliated faculty of the “Slavery North” initiative, and Director of the National Endowment for the Humanities “Landmarks in American History” workshops series for middle- and high school teachers, titled “Sailing to Freedom: New Bedford and the Underground Railroad” (2011-2022). In 2020, Walker was appointed by the Governor of Massachusetts to serve on the Schooner Ernestina/Morrissey Advisory Board, where he is the chair of the Educational Programming Committee.

A Sustainable Future for Nantucket’s Built Heritage

The Nantucket Historical Association (NHA) has partnered with several heritage conservation organizations: International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property (ICCROM), Integrated Conservation Resources Inc. and Integrated Conservation Contracting, Inc. (ICR-ICC), and the Weitzman School of Design at the University of Pennsylvania to assist in developing a disaster and climate risk management plan for its historical assets. This new initiative brings private and public partners together to apply an integrated framework for the assessment of Nantucket’s most important historic properties and by extension, all such assets on the island. A graduate student internship program has been created in Summer 2023 to begin a preliminary survey and assessment of the approximately 20 historic properties of the NHA, (in addition to several other representative historic properties on the island) including past site (legacy) records and structural and material assessments as well as environmental context. Together with regional climate data, this survey will identify the critical factors that are threatening each site and define site vulnerabilities and risks . Such analysis holds the key to more sustainable interventions and long-term preventive conservation and management of these sites and their collections. The program recognizes the unique island laboratory of Nantucket and its potential as a training ground for students and young professionals who will confront these issues in their professional careers. It will also allow the NHA to move forward quickly in a manner that not only protects its historical assets but also satisfies its mission to promote and to educate in heritage conservation and transform those activities into narratives worth sharing with the local community, and other communities both national and international. This presentation summarizes the findings of the 2023 summer internship program and sets the stage to further this research in the coming years with concrete deliverables for protecting and sustaining Nantucket’s built heritage.

Coskata-Coatue: A Refuge on the Edge moderated by Jennifer Karberg

The Coskata-Coatue Wildlife Refuge provides the barrier beach protection that forms Nantucket Harbor, habitat for rare and endangered species, recreation for fishing and birdwatching and a truly wild place on Nantucket Island. In this documentary, the Nantucket Conservation Foundation and the Trustees explore the changing landscape of the Refuge already experiencing climate change impacts. A Q&A session will follow this short film with representatives from the Nantucket Conservation Foundation and the Trustees of Reservations to talk about continuing work and the state of the Refuge this winter. This program is part of the Nantucket Historical Association’s Spring Lecture Series at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. Jen Karberg is a native midwesterner transplanted out to the East Coast. She studied plants at the University of Michigan for her undergrad degree then spent some time working at the Chicago Botanic Garden researching rare plants before heading way up to the Upper Peninsula of Michigan for her graduate degrees. She spent 6 years in the far north studying the ecology of the carnivorous pitcher plant and teaching Wetland Ecology at Michigan Tech University before finishing her Ph.D. in 2008. She then moved out to the Grey Lady in August 2008 to work for NCF as their Research Program Supervisor, helping to organize, plan and oversee the wide variety of research projects we are conducting. Her research interests include wetland ecology, tidal marsh restoration, fire ecology and fire as a management tool, and rare species inventories. Jen is also the chair for the Nantucket Biodiversity Initiative’s Research Grants Program, a founding member of the Sandplain Grassland Network and a board member for the Nantucket Shellfish Association.

A Conversation on Coastal Resilience with Rachael Freeman and Claire Martin

Resilience has quickly become the newest and latest buzzword, but what do we really mean when we talk about coastal resilience? What does coastal resilience look like here on Nantucket? Join Rachael Freeman and Claire Martin as they share a conversation to explore coastal resilience approaches globally, regionally, and locally. The conversation includes an introduction to an adaptive and visionary project here on Nantucket: the design concept for a Washington Street Resilience Framework Plan. This program is part of the Food for Thought Lecture Series at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. Rachael Freeman has worked in the environmental field for over 20 years. She is currently the Director of Environmental & Agricultural Resources for the Nantucket Land Bank where she oversees and participates in planning, project management, and permitting across a wide range of environmental topics. She may also be recognized by her various publications and reports, with subject matters ranging from habitat management to phenology. Rachael grew up visiting her grandparents on Nantucket, and occasionally summered on the island. She moved to Nantucket for a seasonal job with the Nantucket Conservation Foundation in 2003 and has been here ever since. Currently, she and her husband have three children, two dogs, fish, a bearded dragon, and a turtle – it’s a full house! Prior to working at the Land Bank, Rachael was the Research Supervisor at the Nantucket Conservation Foundation and owned and operated Laurentide Environmental, a small environmental consulting company. Rachael holds a Masters of Science in Plant Biology from the University of New Hampshire. Claire Martin was a seasonal Nantucket resident during her undergraduate years at Saint Michael’s College in Colchester, Vermont where she earned her degree in Media Studies, Journalism and Digital Arts. She’s lived on and off the island since 2012, returning in the spring of 2020 to join the Remain Nantucket team as Project Manager. Through her work at Remain, Claire seeks to identify and foster opportunities for community-led coastal resilience collaborations and oversees day-to-day communications for Remain Nantucket and Remain Ventures to effectively communicate Remain’s mission, programs and specific initiatives with the Nantucket community and beyond. For the last three years, she has been managing the Envision Resilience Challenge program, a semester-long design studio that connects interdisciplinary teams from leading universities with coastal communities to envision adaptive and creative solutions to sea level rise. Prior to joining Remain, Claire served as Communications Manager for NatureBridge in California. With campuses in five national parks, NatureBridge’s mission is to connect young people to the wonder and science of the natural world to inspire self-discovery and stewardship of the planet.

“Nantucket: A Front Row Seat for Climate Change Impacts” with Rich Delaney

Whales Tales Lecture Series, June 19, 2018, at the Nantucket Whaling Museum The waters of the Gulf of Maine and northwest Atlantic Ocean have the dubious distinction of have the fastest warming ocean surface water temperatures in the world! This affords us a “front row seat” for understanding and then adapting to very significant coastal and ocean impacts due to climate change. These impacts includes shifting habitats for fish and other species, sea level rise and more intense coastal storms and flooding, potential modification of ocean currents and much more. Understanding what’s ahead will enable coastal communities to better prepare for the inevitable impacts and to begin to take actions that are necessary to adapt to the new reality. Richard Delaney, President of the Center for Coastal Studies, will share his experience with and continuing importance of the Paris Climate Agreement on the international level as well as actions that are already underway at the local level on Cape Cod and Nantucket.

Indicators of Climate Change on Nantucket, with Dr. Sarah Bois at the Nantucket Whaling Museum

Food for Thought Lecture Series presented at the Nantucket Whaling Museum, November 2, 2017 The Linda Loring Nature Foundation’s Director of Research and Education Sarah Bois is building a research program investigating the effects of climate change on our native plant communities. As climate change has been shown to shift spring leaf out and flowering times, there are significant implications for the globally rare sandplain grassland and heathland habitats found on Nantucket. In this project, field observations of eight dominant shrub species were paired with twig warming experiments to investigate the potential for species to take advantage of an earlier spring. In investigating common, native shrubs, we seek to understand how a community, driven by its dominant species, may change with warming spring temperatures.

A Walk with Nantucket’s Notable Women

At the Nantucket Whaling Museum, we’ve always been intrigued with Nantucket’s long and proud history of empowering women and we love to tell their stories. From the early settlers and their descendants to later arrivals from many diverse ethnic and racial backgrounds, Nantucket women have been remarkably industrious and independent. Some led social movements in abolition, suffrage and women’s rights. Others were notable in science, medicine, and education reform. In this video, our museum guides tell the stories of some of the lesser known but very notable Nantucket women who ran businesses, raised large families, and helped build our diverse island community. Here we visit the places where they lived and worked. Today, you’ll find that the tradition of extraordinary women continues. Women continue to inspire us in leadership positions as business owners, government officials, nonprofit directors, and in many other community endeavors. Extraordinary Nantucket Women, at the Nantucket Whaling Museum

This 2018 performance at the Nantucket Whaling Museum highlights the lives of fifteen extraordinary women from the 17th through the 20th century on Nantucket. From its earliest days, dating back to the mid-1600s, Nantucketers have made their own way in the world. This is particularly true of the women who made their homes here. From the outset, men and women worked equally hard to make the fledgling settlement survive. When whaling became the dominant industry, whaling husbands would leave the island for years at a time, often, 3-5 years. At any given time, the women probably outnumbered the men four to one. Women had to fill the breach and did so in remarkable ways, raising their large families, managing households and running businesses in town, and found the time to become involved in the social movements of the day. William Oliver Stevens, an American author and professor, wrote, “Indeed, it is probable that no other community in America of the size of Nantucket has ever given the country so many extraordinary women.” The notable women include: Mary Coffin Starbuck (1645-1717) Abiah Folger Franklin (1667-1752) Kezia Folger Coffin (1772-1798) Lucretia Coffin Mott (1793-1880) Eliza Ann Chase McCleave (1811-1895) Susan Veeder (1816-1897) Maria Mitchell (1818-1889) Rebecca Ann Johnson (1829-??) Mary Ellen Pleasant (ca. 1812-1904) Eliza Starbuck Barney (1802-1889) Anna Gardner (1816-1901) Lydia Folger Fowler, M.D. (1822-1879) Margaret Getchell (1841-1880) Hanna Monaghan (1889-1972) Mildred Jewitt “Madaket Millie” (1907-1990) Also featuring the “Nantucket Girl’s Song” based on a witty poem found in the journal kept by Eliza Brock, wife of Peter C. Brock, master of the Nantucket ship Lexington on a whaling voyage from May 1853 to June 1856. It sums up how many women felt about their husbands being off on whaling voyages for years at a time. Songwriter Susan J. Berman set this poem to music and added a verse of her own.

Extraordinary Nantucket Woman: Wonoma, Wampanoag Healer and Legendary Hero

Wonoma (mid-1600s), the daughter of Wauwinet (and granddaughter of Nickanoose), was a young Wampanoag woman with knowledge of medicinal plants and their healing powers. Island legend, memorialized in 1876 in a poem by Nantucket poet Charlotte P. Baxter, tells of the maiden Wonoma, whose skills as a healer were known even among the western people, who lived beyond the tribal dividing line of Madequecham Valley. This is a love story that tells of Wonoma’s heroism in preventing war between two Nantucket sachems. Produced for the Nantucket Historical Association for the 2010 exhibition “Sometimes think of me: Notable Nantucket Women through the Centuries” at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Extraordinary Nantucket Woman: Phebe Folger Coleman, Artist, Needleworker, Poet

Born to Walter Folger and Elizabeth Starbuck on Nantucket, Phebe Folger Coleman (1771–1857) was one of eight children in a remarkably talented and well-educated family. A close companion to her brother, island genius Walter Folger Jr., she was his intellectual partner, studying mathematics, history, French, and other subjects. In 1797, she became schoolmistress of a Quaker school on the island where she inspired many young girls’ needlework samplers. Examples of Phebe’s artwork, needlework, and poetry have been preserved, showcasing her multiple talents. Phebe married Samuel Coleman in 1798 and together they had three children. She turned all of her skills to her domestic situation – and to the benefit of her husband’s business enterprises. Samuel’s success as a mariner and trader was in large part due to his wife, who taught him navigation. It seems there was nothing Phebe could not do. And if her circumstances had been different – without a husband and children to care for – she might have made history as a scientist, an inventor, a poet, an artist. In 1809, Phebe and Samuel sold their Nantucket house and moved to a farm near Ghent, New York. This video features a poem she wrote later that year, lamenting leaving her elderly parents, her brother, Walter, and her sisters. Produced for the Nantucket Historical Association for the 2010 exhibition “Sometimes think of me: Notable Nantucket Women through the Centuries” at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Extraordinary Nantucket Woman: Eliza Spencer Brock, Whaling Journalist, Poet

Eliza Spencer Brock (1810-1899), wife of Captain Peter C. Brock (1805−78), kept a journal aboard the whaleship Lexington during a voyage from 1853 to 1856. The journey took her to the Azores, Cape Verde Islands, New Zealand, Hawaii, and throughout the South Pacific. In her journal, Eliza expressed the isolation she felt at sea, noting poignantly, “. . . if it was not for hope the heart would break” noting often of her dreams of her home on Nantucket. Eliza included some eighty-five poems and snippets of verse in her journal, some of which she wrote. But the particular poem that has created a stir among scholars of women’s history is the “Nantucket Girls Song,” dated February 1855 that Eliza attributes to Mrs. Martha Ford, Bay of Islands, New Zealand after having tea with her there. Produced for the Nantucket Historical Association for the 2010 exhibition “Sometimes think of me: Notable Nantucket Women through the Centuries” at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Extraordinary Nantucket Woman: Elizabeth Morse Morey, Whaling Journalist, Illustrator

Elizabeth Morse Morey (1810-1893), wife of whaling Captain Israel Morey, kept a journal aboard the whaleship Phoenix during a voyage from 1853 to 1855. Phoenix crossed the Atlantic Ocean, rounded Cape Horn, and hunted for whales in the Pacific Ocean and later the Sea of Okhotsk. A kind, curious woman of a poetic nature, Betsey, as she was known to all, displayed a fascination with the diverse flora and fauna encountered during the voyage and the changing beauties of the sea. Known for a fondness for animals, children, and all living creatures, she felt a special sympathy for the whales captured by the crew and wrote tributes and invented colorful names for many of them. During the course of the voyage, Betsey named all thirty whales taken. In this video, we hear her tributes to the animals she encountered, especially to “Mr. Hogg,” a hog brought on board from Pitt’s Island, and later slaughtered by the crew Produced for the Nantucket Historical Association for the 2010 exhibition “Sometimes think of me: Notable Nantucket Women through the Centuries” at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Click Here to Watch

Extraordinary Nantucket Woman: Susan Austin Veeder, Whaling Voyage Journalist

From September 1848 to March 1853, Susan Austin Veeder (1816-1897) sailed with her husband, Captain Charles A. Veeder, on a whaling voyage aboard the ship Nauticon. The journey took her around Cape Horn to ports in Chile and then to Oahu, Tahiti, and as far north as the Fox Islands in the Arctic. Susan was the first of the Nantucket whaling women to keep a journal. She filled it with gentle watercolors creating a chronicle of her experiences with panoramic views of ports as seen from the ship’s deck. In this stunning journal, Veeder records the full range of shipboard events. Whale chases—shipboard accidents—crew mutinies—and the exchange of supplies and gossip (called a gam by the sailors) with passing ships and local peoples. In this video, we listen to her record of the birth of her own child, “a fine daughter weighing 9 lbs.” and her child’s tragic death. Produced for the Nantucket Historical Association for the 2010 exhibition “Sometimes think of me: Notable Nantucket Women through the Centuries” at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Click Here to Watch

Extraordinary Nantucket Woman: Eunice Ross, African American Student Activist for Education Rights

Communities across America in the 1840s saw the bitter divisions of slavery and racial prejudice dominate public debate. On Nantucket in 1840, Eunice Ross (1824-1895), a seventeen-year-old student of Anna Gardner at the African School, by vote of a town meeting was denied admission to the Nantucket High School because of her race. Five years of hot debate followed the ban, bringing to light ugly prejudices and deeply ingrained fears within the community. Finally, in 1845, frustrated by the delays of the Nantucket School Committee, Edward J. Pompey and 104 other black citizens, including members of the Ross family, submitted a petition to the Massachusetts State House requesting that admission to public schools be extended to all children. In this video, we hear Eunice Ross’s own petition to the legislature requesting equal educational opportunity. Such legislation eventually passed in 1845, but it was not until 1847 that children from the African School, including Eunice Ross and Phoebe Ann Boston, daughter of African American whaling caption, Absalom Boston, were admitted to Nantucket High School. Produced for the Nantucket Historical Association for the 2010 exhibition “Sometimes think of me: Notable Nantucket Women through the Centuries” at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Click Here to Watch

Extraordinary Nantucket Women: Gertrude and Hanna Monaghan, Quakers, Artists, Designers

Gertrude (1887-1962) and Hanna Monaghan (1889-1972), natives of Philadelphia, came to Nantucket in the summers to immerse themselves in art beginning in 1923, when they rented a small cottage-studio joining Nantucket’s thriving art colony in the 1920s and ’30s. They attracted some attention when they drove around town in their chauffeur-driven car, accompanied by their white greyhound named Angel Gabriel, and when they began to remodel an ancient livestock barn and pig sty on Howard Street into a home, it aroused the curiosity of the townspeople, who found them “peculiar.” The sisters wanted to make it perfectly clear that what they accomplished was for the sake of art, and was ultimately an expression of their faith in their inner light. They named their retreat Greater Light. It came to be recognized as a major work of design and decoration. Hanna Monaghan bequeathed Greater Light and its furnishings to the Nantucket Historical Association in 1972. Closed to the public in 2009 for restoration, it was reopened in 2011 as a monument to Nantucket’s Art Colony, and to the era between the two world wars when artists flocked to the island for summers of intense work and instruction. Produced for the Nantucket Historical Association for the 2010 exhibition “Sometimes think of me: Notable Nantucket Women through the Centuries” at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Phebe Ann Coffin Hanaford: A Force from Nantucket

Phebe Hanaford (1829-1921), born on Nantucket, was a friend of Lucretia Mott and Anna Gardner. She was a passionate crusader for equal rights, which she understood to mean both emancipation, education and integration for people of African heritage, and also securing voting rights for women. Her collection of women’s organization pins shows the breadth of her engagement, leading to the passage of the 19th Amendment to the Constitution of the United States.

“Miss Parker”: Clara Parker, Nantucket Atheneum Head Librarian, “New Voter”

“Miss Parker” is a biography of former Nantucket Atheneum head librarian Clara Parker (1877-1970) who held this position for fifty years, serving three generations of Nantucket readers. It also explores Parker’s role as one of the first women on Nantucket to vote in the landmark national election of 1920. The film features a voiceover from acclaimed author Nathaniel Philbrick. Nantucket Lightship Basketmaking Online with Kathleen Myers

The Nantucket Historical Association (NHA) is excited to announce the launch of a new Online Heritage Craft workshop, “Nantucket Lightship Basketmaking,” the first of its kind to teach the process from start to finish. The lightship basket is often viewed as the most notable craft form originating from Nantucket, and is a cornerstone workshop at the NHA. This new online Nantucket basketmaking workshop is designed to be accessible to all, allowing beginners and experienced weavers to enjoy Heritage Craft programming from the comfort of their own home. This new Nantucket basketmaking workshop has been in high demand since the NHA launched online workshops in 2021. It includes pre-recorded video lessons and a kit that contains all the materials packaged needed to create a traditional Nantucket lightship basket. The workshop is taught by master basketmaker, Kathleen Myers, who effortlessly shares six decades of weaving knowledge throughout the course. The online course is available at https://heritagecraftonline.nha.org/. Kathleen Myers has been weaving baskets since the 1960s. She was introduced to Nantucket lightship baskets in the 1980s at a workshop in Michigan. She traveled to Nantucket in 1990s to study part-time with established basket weavers earning a “spot on the bench” at Nantucket Basket Works in 1996. She moved permanently to Nantucket in 1997 and set up shop for herself, where she continues creating baskets through private commissions. Today she is a recognized master basketmaker along with her mentors Tim Parsons, Karol Linquist, Nap Plank, and Alan S.W. Reed. Learn more about Kathleen Myers and her approach to her craft at https://youtu.be/FpdGBJeIeW4.

Behind the Seams Exhibition with Jennifer Nieling at the Nantucket Whaling Museum

Guest curator Jennifer Nieling discusses the making of and inspirations for Behind the Seams, the 2025 featured exhibition at the Nantucket Whaling Museum, from the inventory of the NHA’s costume and textile collection that made the exhibition possible to bringing it to life with costume mounting. Behind the Seams will present over 150 objects from the NHA’s costume and textile collections to tell stories of making, meaning, and island identity from across Nantucket history. Learn how themes of making and meaning emerged through close examination of clothing and textiles in the NHA collection, and how these objects reveal insights into many aspects of history and peoples’ lives. From the materials, trade, and sewing techniques that produced them to what they can tell us about community, identity, and Nantucket history, Nieling will share stories behind objects that made it into the exhibition (and some that didn’t!). She will also illustrate how sustainable practices are visible throughout the historic clothing and textile collection and continue today. Jennifer Nieling is an independent costume and textile specialist with a focus on costume exhibition and display whose association with the NHA goes back to 2015 when she inventoried the menswear collection and mounted the first of many costumes for NHA exhibition projects. In 2017, she led an IMLS-funded inventory and rehousing of the NHA’s clothing and textile collection. Nieling holds a Master of Arts in Fashion & Textile Studies: History, Theory, and Museum Practice from the Fashion Institute of Technology and a Bachelor of Arts from Boston University and has worked at a variety of institutions including the Philadelphia Museum of Art and Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. She started her business JLN Costume Mounting LLC in 2020 and has mounted costumes for the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures, Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture, Science History Institute, Portland Art Museum, and more. She continues to pursue independent research and has published on the history of Nantucket Looms and weaver Andy Oates.

Nantucket Threads: How the NHA Turned Me into a Textile Historian with Isabella Rosner

This talk given by Isabella Rosner at the Nantucket Whaling Museum blends the personal and historical to trace how a summer internship at the Nantucket Historical Association led to a career in textile history. The talk is an exploration of Nantucket’s embroidery history, traversing stories of the Nantucket School of Needlery, Erica Wilson, and contemporary Nantucket embroiderers such as Susan Boardman before concluding with a foray into Nantucket’s Quaker needlework. She hosts the successful Sew What? podcast about historic needlework and those who stitched it, and as a 2023 BBC/AHRC New Generation Thinker, regularly speaks on national radio in the UK. Isabella wrote her PhD on early Quaker women’s waxwork, shellwork, and needlework of the 17th and 18th centuries. Hailing from Los Angeles and now living in London, Isabella counts her internship at the NHA as the opportunity that led her to become a textile historian.

Mid-century Embroidery, Gender, and the Hidden History of Home Study with Rebecca Tolley

In the decades following World War II, embroidery correspondence courses quietly reshaped the domestic craft landscape in the United States. These programs-delivered through the mail ­allowed women across the country to access artistic instruction, vocational training, and creative community from within their homes. This talk explores how mid-century needlework courses bridged leisure and labor, revealing how embroidery functioned as both an expressive art form and a pathway to economic empowerment. Drawing from early research into archival collections-including those of Mary Ann Beinecke and the Nantucket School of Needlery, this lecture examines how such programs reflect larger questions of gender, class, and access in postwar America. It also considers the regional influence of Massachusetts and New York educators such as Mary Ann Beinecke, Erica Wilson, and Nellie Bergh in shaping national craft education. Please note: This presentation offers a snapshot of work in progress. What I share today represents the early contours of a larger research project still unfolding. Rebecca Tolley is an educator, artist, and lifelong learner. She supports research and learning as a professor and academic librarian at East Tennessee State University and has taught Introduction to Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies since 2011. She taught postgraduate courses in trauma-informed librarianship for the American Library Association, trauma-informed librarianship and feminist librarianship for Library Juice, and trauma-informed library leadership as part of the Library Institute for Academic Librarianship at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. Her book A trauma-informed approach to library services (2020) is used as a textbook in library and information science graduate programs at Syracuse University, Emporia State University, and the University of South Carolina. A 2024 SouthArts Emerging Traditional Artists Program fellow for her quiltmaking, Tolley used her award to deepen her knowledge under the guidance of Mary Ann and China Pettway of Gee’s Bend Quilts in Alabama. She regularly teaches and studies improvisational quiltmaking at Shakti in the Mountains, a women’s community center in Johnson City, TN. Through the Tennessee Arts Commission’s Folklife Institute, she facilitated Stitching through Storms: Quilts of Resilience and Recovery, a community quilt block project that memorializes the impact of Hurricane Helene on Northeast Tennessee communities. Her current research explores the overlooked history of mid-century embroidery correspondence courses, with special attention to their cultural, educational, and economic significance in postwar America.

Chair Caning with Liz Coffin

Nantucket House Histories of Noted Nantucket Basket Makers with Mary Bergman

Mary Bergman, Executive Director of Nantucket Preservation Trust, shares house research done by NPT on three houses with connections to noted basket makers. 5 Mill Street, one-time home of Mitchy Ray, was later purchased by notable Nantucket lightship basket collector Eleanor Ham, sister-in-law of Jose Reyes, and great friend of scrimshander Althea Macy. 4 Pine Street was the home of basket maker Frederick Chadwick. And 97 Orange Street was the home of basket maker Ferdinand Sylvaro. Mary shares her process of determining these connections and more. She also shares information on how to go about doing research on your own house. Presented by the Nantucket Lightship Basket Museum, now an affiliation with the Nantucket Historical Association.

Taking Care of Your Nantucket Lightship Basket with Kathleen Myers

Genealogy Tips & Tricks Workshop, Nantucket Historical Association

Archivists Charmaine Bonner and Jessica Salow of Arizona State University lead a workshop for beginners on the basics of genealogical and archival research. They will cover primary source materials, helpful databases, and other resources available to assist you in your family research on Nantucket and beyond. Presented by the Nantucket Historical Association. Charmaine Bonner is the Processing Archivist at Arizona State University Library. Bonner is responsible for arranging, describing, accessioning, and re-boxing manuscript collections. After a collection is physically processed, she writes a finding aid for each collection to describe the collection’s content & other important information. She obtained her Masters Degree in Library Science at North Carolina Central University. Jessica Salow is currently a Specialist at Arizona State University Library with the Community-Driven Archives Initiative (CDA) which was established in 2017 through the generous support of The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation. She obtained her Masters in Library and Information Science (MLIS) from The University of Arizona and is an alumna of Arizona State University.

Research Your Nantucket House History Workshop

Let us help you discover your Nantucket home’s story! Learn how to research the history of your own home or other historic properties, using resources available through the Nantucket Historical Association, Nantucket Atheneum, Nantucket Town Records, and more, using 27 York Street (the Boston–Higginbotham House) as an example. The panel is moderated by Mary Bergman, Executive Director of Nantucket Preservation Trust with panelists, Betsy Tyler, author, NHA Research Fellow, and former Obed Macy Research Chair; Lincoln Thurber, Nantucket Atheneum Head Reference Librarian; and Amelia Holmes, NHA Director of Collections & Research Services. Presented by the Nantucket Historical Association. Co-sponsored by Housing Nantucket; the Museum of African American History, Boston and Nantucket; and the Nantucket Preservation Trust.

Tuckernuck, an Interview with Ruth Chapel Grieder

Ruth Chapel Grieder (1927-2016) was born on Nantucket, spending the summers of her infancy and early years on Tuckernuck in the 1930s. Ruth can trace back five generations of her family born and raised on Tuckernuck and shares her memories of ’living in paradise“ along with memories of her family. This excerpt is taken from a 2007 oral history interview for the Nantucket Historical Association. To learn more about Tuckernuck, listen to the NHA podcast ”When The Fog Comes Drifting In“ - Tuckernuck Island with Susie Robinson at https://youtu.be/8KBEEb1tNDQ.

Nantucket-Cape Verde Connection: Heritage

Heritage: “Our grandchildren need to know that we’re proud to be Cape Verdean.” People of the Cape Verde archipelago and their descendants have been part of the story of Nantucket since the early nineteenth century. While diminished in numbers from early days, the Nantucket Cape Verdean community today is made up of significant contributors to education, health care, service to the community, government, business, trades, music, and cuisine, assuring that anyone in their expanded spheres are well fed. They are a microcosm of the best of Nantucket’s community spirit, subtly proud of their Cape Verde heritage. This short film is based on recently conducted oral histories with members of Nantucket’s Cape Verdean community. Special thanks to those who shared their stories: Kenneth DeLuze, Dominic Duarte, Kezia Duarte, Mary Fernandes, Anthony “Rocky” Fox, Viola Cabral Howard, Leslie Gomes Preston, Edmund “Rookie” Ramos, Pauline Cabral Singleton, Theran Singleton, and Claudia Stanley. Interviews conducted by Frances Karttunen for the Nantucket Historical Association. Learn more about the Nantucket-Cape Verde connection at https://nha.org/research/nantucket-history/history-topic/cape-verdean-heritage-on-nantucket/. Music: “Morna di Freddie” performed by Verdatones

Billy Baldwin - Nantucket Influences

Billy Baldwin (William Williar Baldwin, Jr., 1903-1983) , famously known as the dean of American interior decorators, summered on and off Nantucket Island since childhood and retired here in 1973, a decade before his death. In this excerpt from an interview done for the Nantucket Historical Association and Nantucket Channel 3 in 1976, he shares a few memories and experiences as a child with his family in ‘Sconset during their summer holidays. He also discusses certain subtle influences that later emerged in his exemplary design aesthetic. Archival interview footage from the Film Collection of the Nantucket Historical Association. The full interview can be viewed at https://youtu.be/9-DtuuPuFIE .

Albert Ottison, Nantucket Boat Builder

Albert Ottison (1915-2010) was well known on island for his skill in building wooden boats. He built work boats and pleasure boats, often using wood cut from trees, salvaged from Steamboat Wharf, or found at the dump. His son, Karl Ottison, talked with us about his dad’s skills and passion for building boats. Produced by John Stanton, Shouldered Oar Films, for the Nantucket Historical Association, 2018.

Marylane and Delber Branco, from Brazil to Nantucket

Marylane and Delber Branco, Brazil Interview Date: November 29, 2013 Interviewer: Nancy Newhouse The Brancos moved from Rio de Janiero to Nantucket in 1998. They share a story about crossing cultures. The Nantucket Historical Association’s oral-history project New Voices: Nantucket’s Diverse Immigrant Populations, is made possible in part by a grant from Mass Humanities. records the experiences of people from around the world who have moved to Nantucket to seek jobs, to provide a better education for their children, and to live in a safe and beautiful place. They have contributed their full stories and photograph selections to the oral history archive of the Nantucket Historical Association. This project was made possible in part by a grant from Mass Humanities.

Here they discuss hope and sacrifice for their family on Nantucket. The Nantucket Historical Association’s oral-history project New Voices: Nantucket’s Diverse Immigrant Populations, is made possible in part by a grant from Mass Humanities. records the experiences of people from around the world who have moved to Nantucket to seek jobs, to provide a better education for their children, and to live in a safe and beautiful place. They have contributed their full stories and photograph selections to the oral history archive of the Nantucket Historical Association. This project was made possible in part by a grant from Mass Humanities.

The Sconset Volunteer Fire Department on Nantucket Island

In this mini-documentary produced by filmmaker John Stanton for the Nantucket Historical Association, current ‘Sconset residents share stories about the Siasconset Volunteer Fire Department. It includes excerpts from a series of oral histories conducted by John Stanton for the NHA in 2019. In this video, Snookie Eldridge remembers joining the ‘Sconset Fire Department in 1959. Snookie and Rob Benchely talk about what it was like to serve as a volunteer, responding to calls in the middle of the night, having to know where the house alarms were located and where the keys were hidden, and doing whatever was necessary to help get the fires under control. The ‘Sconset Fire Department was disbanded in 2015 when Rob, the youngest volunteer, was 65. The ’Sconset Oral History Project was generously funded by the Judy Family Foundation.

Sconset Market on Nantucket Island

In this mini-documentary produced by filmmaker John Stanton for the Nantucket Historical Association, current ‘Sconset residents share stories of the ‘Sconset Market. It includes excerpts from a series of oral histories conducted by John Stanton for the NHA in 2019. In this video, Snookie Eldridge talks about the local businesses run by John Salvas in the original building before it became the ‘Sconset Market. Mark Donato talks about managing the market on trial at the beginning, purchasing it in 1982, and finally selling it in 2017. Jennie and Nathanael Greene remember working there—Mark shares that for three generations, he gave any kid who wanted a summer job at least a small one. Mark also talks about instituting a very popular “credit system” and how it met its demise. The ’Sconset Oral History Project was generously funded by the Judy Family Foundation.

Moving Sankaty Lighthouse in Sconset on Nantucket Island

In this mini-documentary produced by filmmaker John Stanton for the Nantucket Historical Association, current ‘Sconset residents tell the story of the moving of Sankaty Lighthouse back from the ‘Sconset bluff to safe ground in 2007. It includes excerpts from a series of oral histories conducted by John Stanton for the NHA in 2019. In this video, Bob Felch, former Executive Director of ‘Sconset Trust, was responsible for organizing the move and also for fundraising. He recalls that it took a village and how funds and other support not only came in from ‘Sconset residents, but from all of Nantucket, and throughout the country. Bob says, “There was nothing negative about it, nothing political about it. It was all good.” Photojournalist Rob Benchley, who lived on Baxter Road and could see the lighthouse from his home, was granted access throughout the move to document the historic event. The video features some of his photography from that time. The ’Sconset Oral History Project was generously funded by the Judy Family Foundation.

Wade Cottages in Sconset on Nantucket Island

This mini-documentary, produced by filmmaker John Stanton for the Nantucket Historical Association, includes excerpts from a series of oral histories conducted by John for the NHA in 2019. In this video, in-season ‘Sconset residents Nathanael and Jennie Greene talk about how their great grandparents purchased the Wade Cottages in the 1920s for use as a family compound – and how that morphed after the depression into a family business renting guest rooms and cottages. The cottage rentals continue today. They remember summers living there around the needs of guests and the extended summer season they enjoyed. They also talk about how they remembered Codfish Park and how it has evolved from a year-round community, through the loss of many beach-front cottages to erosion, and is now more an enclave of summer residents. The ’Sconset Oral History Project was generously funded by the Judy Family Foundation.

Sankaty Bluff Erosion in Sconset on Nantucket Island

How I Got Here - to Sconset on Nantucket Island

In this mini-documentary produced by filmmaker John Stanton for the Nantucket Historical Association, current ’Sconset residents share their memories of how they came to live in Sconset. It includes excerpts from a series of oral histories conducted by John Stanton for the NHA in 2019. In this video, actor John Shea talks about leaving Town and moving to ’Sconset as a hippy in the 70s. Bob Felch moved from the mid-west and “married” into ’Sconset—his wife’s family had ties back to the 19-teens when a railroad ran out to ’Sconset. Mark Donato and his wife moved from Idaho to open the Morning Glory Café and lived above the ’Sconset Market. Martha Holdgate Butler is a ’Sconset native. Paul Judy celebrated his 50th summer in Sconset. Rob Benchley talks about “a great clump of Dickinsons and Benchleys that invaded ’Sconset” starting in the 30s. And more . . . The ’Sconset Oral History Project was generously funded by the Judy Family Foundation.

Chanticleer Restaurant and The Moby Dick Inn, Sconset on Nantucket Island

In this mini-documentary produced by filmmaker John Stanton for the Nantucket Historical Association, ‘Sconset residents share their memories of and experiences with the historic Chanticleer Restaurant, still open today, and the Moby Dick Inn, fondly remembered but no longer in existence. It includes excerpts from a series of oral histories conducted by John Stanton for the NHA in 2019. In this video, Bob Felch and Paul Judy recall the history and prior owners of the Chanticleer, how it became a first-class French restaurant, and how a group of Sconset residents, feeling it an important part of the Sconset community, saved it from being turned into a private home. John Shea worked at both the Chanticleer and the Moby Dick and compares his experiences in both work places. The ’Sconset Oral History Project was generously funded by the Judy Family Foundation.

Billy Baldwin, Summering in ’Sconset on Nantucket Island

Billy Baldwin (William Williar Baldwin, Jr., 1903-1983) , famously known as the dean of American interior decorators, summered on and off Nantucket Island since childhood and retired here in 1973, a decade before his death. In this interview done for the Nantucket Historical Association and Nantucket Channel 3 in 1976, he talks about his memories and experiences as a child with his family in ‘Sconset during their summer holidays. He also discusses certain subtle influences that later emerged in his exemplary design aesthetic. Archival interview footage and cover portrait from the collections of the Nantucket Historical Association. Written on the reverse of the watercolor portrait: “Billy Baldwin by his cousin Rita.”

The Srail Club

This mini-documentary about the Srail Club in ’Sconset was produced for the 2008 exhibition ’Sconset 02564 at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. It includes excerpts from a series of oral histories of ’Sconset residents conducted by the NHA in 1976 and 2007 along with archival video and photos on the topic. In this video, Gibbs Penrose (1908-76) shows the building’s location and explains that “Srail” backwards is “liars.” Joan Brown Porter (1930-) talks about how her grandfather Lee Parsons Davis, a New York state supreme court judge started the Srail Club in 1930 with the intention of making it a haven for “tall tales.” But the spirit of club was that year-round and summer members were equal and all were welcome, even from far-off Nantucket. Joan describes further some of the antics that went on there.

Walter Folger (1924-2017) remembers dining there and the shows in the cocktail lounge with headline performers from Broadway. Joan Brown Porter (1930-) remembers “Tiny,” a rather large man who played the piano. And she remembers the red glow the night the inn burned down. Sankaty Head Lighthouse

This mini-documentary about the Sankaty Head Lighthouse in ’Sconset was produced for the 2008 exhibition ’Sconset 02564 at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. It includes excerpts from a series of oral histories of ’Sconset residents conducted by the NHA in 1976 and 2007 along with archival video and photos on the topic. Joan Pennock Craig (1920-2011) remembers lighthouse keeper Eugene Larson taking local kids to the top and enjoying the view. Walter Folger (1924-2017) remembers when the Coast Guard wanted to eliminate the cage at the top in favor of an open beacon, but local sentiment changed the decision. Linda Holland (1939-) fondly remembers morning yoga at the lighthouse with Marta Green—and shooting pool at the light keeper’s house. Joan Brown Porter (1930-) recalls the original cost of building the lighthouse. And Bob Longley (1932-2013) remembers the delight of seeing Sankaty light coming over Bean Hill when returning to ’Sconset each summer.

Clarence Wilson, ’Sconset Personality

This mini-documentary about ‘Sconset resident Clarence Wilson and his family was produced for the 2008 exhibition ’Sconset 02564 at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. It includes excerpts from an audio oral history of ’Sconset resident Joan Wilson Godeau (1936-) conducted by the NHA in 2008 and includes archival video and photos on the topic. Joan recalls how her father came to ‘Sconset as butler to the Houston family in 1938 and her mother followed in 1941 as a personal maid, bringing Joan along at age 4. My Folks Came to ’Sconset in . . .

This mini-documentary about how folks first came to ’Sconset was produced for the 2008 exhibition ’Sconset 02564 at the Nantucket Whaling Museum. It includes excerpts from a series of oral histories of ’Sconset residents conducted by the NHA in 1976 and 2007-8 along with archival video and photos on the topic. In this video, Joan Brown Porter (1930-) tells of her folks’ first coming in 1886 because Nantucket was “allergy-free.” Bob Longley’s (1932-2013) grandfather, Harry Longley, an Episcopal bishop, first summered in ’Sconset in 1896. Gibbs Penrose (1908-76) was brought to ’Sconset by his actor parents the year he was born. Billy Baldwin (1903-84) first came to visit his aunt in 1913. Joan Pennock Craig (1920-2011) came with her family in 1923, invited by the Beinecke family. Grace Stanshigh Yates (1932-2015) was born on Nantucket and lived in ’Sconset all her life. Linda Holland (1939-) came here through her mother’s connection with the Wades of Wade Cottages. Walter Folger (1924-2017) started summering here as a boy at his grandparent’s home on King Street, but his sister, Sheila Folger Todd (1936-), arrived within weeks of her birth. Nan Dempster Longley (1934-) and her brother were brought here to avoid the polio epidemic in New York. Margaret Fawcett Barnes (1896-1980) was brought here as a baby to recover from malaria.
